sources.design: meta-analysis of clinical vs. mechanical prediction studies
sources.effect: ~10% accuracy advantage for mechanical prediction; substantially outperformed clinical in 33-47% of studies
sources.finding_quote: On average, mechanical-prediction techniques were about 10% more accurate than clinical predictions. Depending on the specific analysis, mechanical prediction substantially outperformed clinical prediction in 33%-47% of studies examined. Although clinical predictions were often as accurate as mechanical predictions, in only a few studies (6%-16%) were they substantially more accurate. Superiority for mechanical-prediction techniques was consistent, regardless of the judgment task, type of judges, judges' amounts of experience, or the types of data being combined.

sources.cite: Nieuwenstein, Wierenga, Morey, Wicherts, Blom, Wagenmakers & van Rijn (2015)
sources.design: meta-analysis + N=399 pre-registered large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage
sources.effect: no evidence for the effect at adequate power
sources.finding_quote: Consistent with the reliability account, the large-scale replication study yielded no evidence for the UTA, and the meta-analysis showed that previous reports of the UTA were confined to underpowered studies that used relatively small sample sizes... we conclude that there exists no reliable support for the claim that a momentary diversion of thought leads to better decision making than a period of deliberation.

backfire.condition: Analyzing/verbalizing reasons for a preference shifts choice toward reasons that are easy to articulate but not the true determinants of quality, reducing agreement with experts.
Criteria for merit can be constructed after the fact to justify a preferred option, undermining decomposition's consistency benefit if criteria are chosen after an initial holistic reaction.

sources.design: 36 independent samples, N=6,344, 13 classic effects including 4 anchoring items
sources.effect: anchoring replicated with larger effect sizes than originals (weighted d = 1.17-2.42 vs original d = 0.93)
sources.finding_quote: Although replication is a central tenet of science, direct replications are rare in psychology. backfire.condition: Insufficient-adjustment mechanism is specific to self-generated anchors (relevant to whether writing the gut score first neutralises or reproduces anchoring); no direct test of the page's reorder-to-neutralise logic was found.

sources.effect: consider-the-opposite reduced biased assimilation more than be-unbiased instructions
sources.finding_quote: In both experiments the induction of a consider-the-opposite strategy had greater corrective effect than more demand-laden alternative instructions to be as fair and unbiased as possible.

sources.design: narrative review chapter, Blackwell Handbook of Judgment and Decision Making
sources.effect: consider-the-opposite reduces overconfidence, hindsight bias, and anchoring
sources.finding_quote: the simple but general strategy of 'consider the opposite' [is] impressive, because it has been effective at reducing overconfidence, hindsight biases, and anchoring effects... The strategy consists of nothing more than asking oneself, 'What are some reasons that my initial judgment might be wrong?'... [it] directly counteracts the basic problem of association-based processes—an overly narrow sample of evidence—by expanding the sample and making it more representative.

sources.design: 2 studies; listing 2 vs. 10 counterfactual thoughts
sources.effect: listing many (10) counterfactuals increased hindsight bias via ease-of-retrieval
sources.finding_quote: Listing many counterfactual thoughts was experienced as difficult and consistently increased the hindsight bias, presumably because the experienced difficulty suggested that there were not many ways in which the event might have turned out otherwise. No significant hindsight effects were obtained when participants listed only a few counterfactual thoughts.

backfire.condition: Quantity-dependent reversal: a short list of contrary reasons helps, but a long list (e.g. ten) is experienced as effortful, and that felt difficulty is misread as evidence the original judgement was right, worsening the bias.

sources.design: 2 experiments on confidence and evidence retrieval
sources.effect: confidence tracks amount/strength of retrieved supporting evidence
sources.finding_quote: People are often overconfident in evaluating the correctness of their knowledge... Correlational analyses of the data of Experiment 1 strongly suggested that the confidence depends on the amount and strength of the evidence supporting the answer chosen.

sources.design: measurement review distinguishing metacognitive bias, sensitivity, and efficiency
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: the degree of association between accuracy and confidence can be taken as a quantitative measure of metacognition... we distinguish between the related concepts of metacognitive bias (a difference in subjective confidence despite basic task performance remaining constant), metacognitive sensitivity (how good one is at distinguishing between one's own correct and incorrect judgments) and metacognitive efficiency.

sources.design: reconciliation of overestimation, overplacement, overprecision
sources.effect: overprecision more persistent than the other two overconfidence types
sources.finding_quote: On difficult tasks, people overestimate their actual performances but also mistakenly believe that they are worse than others; on easy tasks, people underestimate their actual performances but mistakenly believe they are better than others... Overprecision appears to be more persistent than either of the other 2 types of overconfidence.

backfire.condition: Overprecision (excess certainty) persists even where the direction of over/underestimation reverses between easy and hard tasks, so 'high confidence' ratings can remain overprecise even when resolution holds in aggregate.

sources.effect: outcome bias replicated with larger effect than original (d=0.77-1.1 vs original d=0.21-0.53)

sources.cite: Flyvbjerg, B. (2013). Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View. International Journal of Project Management.
sources.design: applies Kahneman & Tversky's outside-view theory to project management; reports Lovallo & Kahneman (2003)'s controlled experiment on college students as direct evidence the outside view corrects rather than merely anchors
sources.effect: a simple diversion into outside-view information reduced overconfident forecasts by 20%, moving them toward accuracy
sources.finding_quote: Verbatim, fetched from the full-text PDF, read in full this session. 'The research shows that when people are asked simple questions requiring them to take an outside view, their forecasts become significantly more accurate. For example, a group of students enrolling at a college were asked to rate their future academic performance relative to their peers in their major. On average, these students expected to perform better than 84 percent of their peers, which is logically impossible... Another group of incoming students from the same major were asked about their entrance scores and their peers scores before being asked about their expected performance. This simple diversion into relevant outside-view information, which both groups of subjects were aware of, reduced the second groups average expected performance ratings by 20 percent. That is still overconfident, but it is significantly more realistic than the forecast made by the first group (Lovallo and Kahneman 2003:61).' Boundary condition, same source: the outside view helps 'when forecasters are honestly trying to gauge the future' (optimism-bias case) but has low potential 'where strategic misrepresentation is the main cause of inaccuracy.'

sources.cite: Buehler, R., Griffin, D. & MacDonald, H. (1997). The Role of Motivated Reasoning in Optimistic Time Predictions. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(3), 238-247.
sources.design: task-completion-time predictions; a recall condition prompted participants to recall similar past experiences before predicting; a further manipulation forced participants to actively connect the recalled experience to their current prediction
sources.effect: merely recalling past experience did not reduce optimistic bias; only forcing the past to be treated as relevant did
sources.finding_quote: Not independently fetched verbatim this session (JSTOR/SAGE closed; Semantic Scholar/Unpaywall carry no abstract). DOI verified via CrossRef (title/authors/year match). Reported via a WebSearch synthesis, not a primary quote: 'Only 12% of participants reported thinking about past experiences when making their current plans in the Recall condition (compared to 2% in the Control condition)... attention to and awareness of the past is not enough to make the past relevant to the future... forcing the past to become relevant eliminates the optimistic prediction bias for completion times.' This is the direct evidence for the opposite failure mode from anchoring: a written/recalled reference point that gets ignored rather than over-weighted.

replication.cite: Flyvbjerg (2013), citing Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994) and Gilovich, Griffin & Kahneman (2002)

backfire.condition: Merely writing/recalling a reference-class figure does not guarantee it is used -- people often discount it as inapplicable to their specific case unless forced to actively connect it to the estimate at hand. This is a more likely failure mode for `forecast` than the base rate acting as a sticky anchor.

The outside view corrects accuracy only when forecasters are honestly trying to be accurate; it has little effect when inaccuracy is strategic/motivated (e.g. competitive bids) -- a genuine boundary condition not previously sourced.
